messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Retail Worker
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 59

Elias sits on the edge of the leather chair, hands folded tightly in his lap. He is thirty-six, European, with the quiet exhaustion of a man who has stopped trusting the floor to hold him steady. Three years ago, on a Tuesday in November, he stands inside a sprawling department store where he manages the flooring department. The renovation crew above has compromised a load-bearing beam during a rushed weekend installation. When the concrete gives way, the sound is not a crash but a deep, swallowing groan, followed by a curtain of white dust and the sudden, violent shift of weight. Elias remembers the smell of pulverized drywall and the way the emergency lights flicker like dying fireflies. He remembers crawling under a collapsed display rack, listening to the muffled screams fade into the mechanical whir of stalled escalators. He survives by holding his breath until his lungs burn, pressing himself into the narrow space between a shattered glass partition and a steel support column. In the weeks that follow, the world feels thin, as if reality were a sheet stretched too tight over his ribs. He begins avoiding any building that has recently undergone construction or features exposed ceiling tiles. Grocery stores with low, flat ceilings make him feel the floor tilt beneath his boots. At home, his wife, Clara, notices how he flinches when the radiator clicks or when a book drops from a shelf. He tells himself he is just being careful, but the truth sits heavier in his chest: the ground still feels untrustworthy. He stops sleeping past 3 a.m. He lies awake, replaying the groan of the concrete, calculating how many seconds he had left, wondering if the beam would have held if they had used different supports. His thoughts circle the same fractured logic, convincing him that safety is a myth sold by people who have never watched a ceiling fail. He still works retail, though he transfers to a smaller independent hardware store on the outskirts of town. The shift in daylight and the exposed brick walls help, but the routine becomes his anchor. Every morning, he unlocks the front door, checks the emergency exits, and runs his fingers along the load-bearing walls before ringing the alarm. Customers ask for screwdrivers or paint samples, and he moves with deliberate slowness, measuring the space between himself and the high metal shelving. He likes the weight of a tool in his hand, the predictability of a transaction. But when the overhead intercom crackles to life, his pulse jumps to his throat. He counts the hollow tiles beneath his boots, notes the exact distance to the back door, and reminds himself that metal ducts do not fall. Clara tries to keep him grounded. She leaves his favorite tea on the counter and packs his lunch the way he used to like it. He appreciates it, but sometimes the quiet of the kitchen feels like holding his breath underwater. He wants to tell her about the dreams where the walls close in, but the words catch in his throat like drywall dust. He kisses her forehead when he leaves for work, a gesture of reassurance he is not sure he believes himself. Today, he watches the dust motes drift through the shaft of afternoon light in this office. He notices how the ceiling meets the wall at a perfect, unbroken angle. He wonders if someone checked the structural supports before they poured the concrete, if they followed the blueprints or cut corners for profit. His shoulders drop an inch, then tighten again. He shifts in the chair, adjusts his posture, and places his palms flat against his knees. The moment passes. He breathes in, out, and waits for the question that will bring him back to the floor, back to the dust, back to the long, careful work of learning how to stand.
